title: A giant built just like you
hook: Make a person 10 times bigger, same shape, same bone. Are the legs still up to the job?

doesNotKnow: that weight grows with the cube of size but bone cross-section only with the square
so each square centimetre of bone in a scaled-up body carries more load in proportion to its size

misconception: A giant built exactly like a person, just 10 times larger, would be just as sturdy.
objective: The learner can explain that scaling every length by 10 multiplies weight by 1,000 but bone cross-section by only 100, so load per square centimetre rises 10 times; that much thicker bones would keep it level; and that real large mammals mostly keep bone stress level by posture instead.

claims.text: Scaling every length by k multiplies weight (volume, same material) by k³ and bone cross-section by k², so the load on each square centimetre of bone grows by k: at 10×, weight ×1,000, bone area ×100, load ×10.
claims.source: Geometry of similar solids (prerequisites math:area-scaling, math:volume-scaling); company/domains/briefs/checks/big-ideas-cycle1-check.mjs #3; Demo.tsx scaleOf(). Static axial load only; the model ignores bending and dynamic loads.

claims.text: Galileo argued in 1638 that giants need disproportionately thick bones.
claims.source: Galilei, G. (1638), Discorsi e dimostrazioni matematiche intorno a due nuove scienze (Two New Sciences), Second Day (public domain; the bone figure and passage on giants, section to confirm). Not opened by the builder.

claims.text: Where it stops: big mammals mostly stand more upright instead of growing far thicker bones, which keeps peak bone stress roughly level across sizes.
claims.source: Biewener, A. A. (1989), 'Scaling body support in mammals: limb posture and muscle mechanics', Science 245(4913), 45-48: bone allometry is modest; larger mammals reduce peak stresses mainly through more upright limbs (better mechanical advantage). Holds roughly up to horse size; the largest mammals (elephants) are also slower and less athletic (to confirm). The lesson's one held citation (class H) on the learner path; Galileo (c2, 1638) is public domain (class P). Not opened by the builder. Cut if not checkable; fallback (v2, W-634): the reveal's last paragraph becomes 'Where it stops: real animals change shape and posture as they grow.' (support: convention, illustrated by the stage's 'thicker legs' toggle, c4), with no claim about bone stress in mammals.

claims.text: The limit line (4× today's load) and the thicker-legs model (bone diameter ×k^1.5, so load stays level) are the lesson's illustrations, not measured values.
claims.source: Labelled 'limit (illustrative)' on the stage. 4× is chosen to sit within the 2-4 safety factors reported for limb bones in vigorous activity (Biewener, A. A. (1990), 'Biomechanics of mammalian terrestrial locomotion', Science 250(4984), 1097-1103; to confirm). Thicker legs: diameter ∝ k^1.5 gives cross-section ∝ k³ = weight, so load ×1 (derivation).

claims.text: With same-shape legs, each square centimetre of bone in the 10× giant carries more than the illustrative limit.
claims.source: 10 > 4 (c1, c4). The stage colours the legs and the bar red above the line. The lesson does not claim a 10× giant would collapse standing still: real standing stresses are far below bone strength, and the margin that disappears is the one used in running and jumping (c4).

recall.question: A statue is copied at 3 times the size in every direction, in the same stone. Compared with the original, the pressure on the stone at its base is about…
recall.why: Weight grows 27 times (3³) but the base area only 9 times (3²), so the pressure on each bit of base grows 3 times, the scale factor itself.
